n: Answering the king’s despair, Elisha announces that by this time tomorrow, food will be so plentiful that fine flour and barley will sell cheaply at Samaria’s gate.

f.g: a unit of weight for silver, about 2/5 ounce (11 grams).
the city’s marketplace and public square.

n: A royal officer scoffs: even if the Lord opened windows in the sky, could this happen? Elisha replies that he will see it but not eat any.

f.w: a lord on whose hand the king leaned
f.g: a high officer, the king’s personal aide.

n: Four men with skin disease, forced by law to live outside the city, sit by the gate starving.

f.g: people with skin disease had to live outside the camp or city.

n: Their logic is simple: staying means death, entering the city means death; surrendering to the Arameans might mean life.
At dusk they creep to the Aramean camp and find it completely empty.
The Lord had made the Arameans hear the roar of chariots and a great army. They assumed Israel had hired Hittite and Egyptian armies against them. God won the battle with sound alone.

f.g: rulers of Neo-Hittite states in northern Syria.

n: They fled at dusk, leaving tents, animals, and everything else behind.
The starving lepers eat and drink, then start carrying off silver, gold, and clothing to hide it.
Their consciences stop them: “We are not doing right. This is a day of good news, and we are keeping it to ourselves.” Many readers see a lesson about sharing the gospel’s good news.
They call to the gatekeepers and report the empty camp, with animals still tied up.
The gatekeepers relay the news to the palace.
The king suspects a trick: the Arameans are hiding in ambush to lure the starving Israelites out. Faithless people struggle to believe good news.
An officer suggests sending a few of the remaining horses to scout. Those horses will likely die anyway, he says, like the rest of Israel’s people.
They send two chariot teams to investigate.
The scouts follow the trail all the way to the Jordan, finding it littered with clothing and equipment thrown away in the panic.
The people rush out and plunder the camp. Prices fall exactly as Elisha prophesied.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD

n: The king puts the skeptical officer in charge of the gate, and the stampeding crowd tramples him to death—also as Elisha had said.
The narrator repeats the prophecy to stress that every detail came true.
He also repeats the officer’s mockery and Elisha’s warning.
The officer saw the abundance but never tasted it. Unbelief can cause a person to witness God’s blessings without sharing in them.

f.w: so it fell out unto him
f.g: that is exactly what happened to him.
